title: Unrolled gradients in disguise: bridging interpolation-based and Jacobian regularization for stable neural dynamics
claim: Offline, Jacobian-matching and accumulated-error losses are different truncations of one unrolled-trajectory error, differing in how many steps of error they count.
layout: 1 panel, left-to-right diverging trajectories, colored double-headed arrows mark each loss
description: A single geometric diagram on a white background shows three trajectories fanning out from a starting point x_t on the left. The true trajectory is blue and curves downward, with points x_{t+Δt}, x_{t+2Δt} and x_{t+3Δt}. A brown learned-model rollout F_θ goes upward and ends at x^{θ,t}_{t+3Δt}. A red rollout restarts from the true x_{t+Δt}, so F_θ is applied from the ground-truth state, and sits in the middle. Black X markers with superscript and subscript labels mark the states. Colored double-headed arrows mark the losses. A blue 'Offline' arrow spans the first step. A brown 'AccMatch' arrow spans the full accumulated gap after two steps. A red 'JacMatch/CFO' arrow spans the shorter gap from the restarted trajectory. The eye goes first to the colored arrows and labels.
caption: Losses interpretation. When $\gamma=1$, $x_t^\gamma=x_{t+\Delta t}$ and we get that JacMatch is equivalent to the error of a delayed $F_\theta$ trajectory starting from $x_{t+\Delta t}$, i.e., only accounting for the error between the Jacobians while AccMatch also accounts for the error after the first timestep.
abstract: Hybrid models and neural differential equations (NDEs) are becoming increasingly important for modelling physical systems; however, they often encounter stability and accuracy issues during long-term integration. Training on unrolled trajectories is known to limit these divergences but quickly becomes too computationally expensive due to the need to compute gradients over an iterative process, making this method impractical for large-scale physical systems (e.g. weather and climate forecasting). Two popular paradigms for improving the stability of learned dynamics are to train on interpolated or noisy samples or to regularize the Jacobian of the learned representation. In this work, we demonstrate that these paradigms can be understood under a common lens and that they both correspond to an approximation of the gradients obtained in an unrolled learning strategy. Building on this understanding, we derive a principled and complete approach to regularize training and demonstrate its impact on the stability of learned dynamical systems.
